raw_response:
I have farmed these 30.4 mu for 51 years, and I know every ridge and hollow. My household has eight people, but the younger ones work off-farm in the county town or in Handan, so I cannot count on family labor during the peak seasons. I have a well, which means I do not pray for rain, but electricity for the pump costs money, so I water only when the crop truly needs it.

This year, I will plant all 30.4 mu to winter wheat in October. Wheat is my foundation—it has a government purchase guarantee, the market is stable, and the straw feeds our animals. I will use an improved semi-dwarf variety with good resistance to lodging and stripe rust, because I cannot afford to see the crop flat on the ground after a summer storm. After the summer crops come off, I will use rotary tillage to prepare a fine seedbed, apply base fertilizer, and top-dress urea at green-up and jointing. I will irrigate three times: wintering water in November if the soil is dry, jointing water in early spring, and grain-filling water in May. I will spray twice—once for weeds and once for aphids or fungus at heading. I expect about 550 kg per mu.

After wheat harvest in early June, the window is narrow. I will put 26 mu into hybrid summer maize using no-tillage direct seeding straight into the wheat stubble. No-till saves me precious days and keeps the soil moisture for germination; at 68, I cannot afford to fall behind the weather. Maize pays the best return per mu, so I will side-dress nitrogen at the big trumpet stage and irrigate three times: at sowing if the topsoil is dry, at jointing, and at tasseling/silking. Two pesticide applications will control the corn borer and weeds. On my better soil, I expect 650 kg per mu.

The remaining 4.4 mu I will plant to improved millet. My wife prefers our own millet for porridge, and the northeast corner of my field is sandier and drier—better suited to millet than to thirsty maize. Millet needs less labor, less fertilizer, and only two irrigations and one pesticide spray. I expect 250 kg per mu, which is enough for our household table and some to send home with the children.

I have watched too many neighbors gamble on untested varieties or pour on inputs like water, only to end up with debt and not much more yield. I trust my experience: balanced fertilizer, timely water at the critical stages, and varieties that have proven themselves on this specific land.
